about.heading: About
paragraphs: I'm a software developer in Mogi Mirim, São Paulo, Brazil, with more than ten years in technology. I build complete applications: the screens people use, the logic and data behind them, and the servers they run on. The industry calls that a full-stack developer. In practice it means you can hand me a problem and get back a working system.

I started on the systems most people never see: the mainframes behind AT&T's billing and Bank Safra's core banking, at IBM. That taught me how software has to behave when a business depends on it every second. I then spent five years at Stefanini building websites, company portals and custom tools for international clients such as American Airlines, GSK, Edenred and Sesc.

Today I build and run the internal systems of Rede Zeferino, a supermarket chain in São Paulo state. Store staff use them every day to weigh deliveries, print labels, check equipment and pull reports. I also built the chain's public website and careers page. On the side I make my own apps, such as an expense-splitting app and a tool for bands, and host them on a server I manage myself.

I speak English fluently and Spanish at an intermediate level, and I like teaching: I've given company-wide talks on Docker and WordPress and ran weekly English classes for colleagues. My main tools are PHP (Laravel and WordPress), JavaScript and React, MySQL and Oracle databases, and Docker.

live.title: Rede Zeferino — Company Website & Careers Page
live.description: The public website of a supermarket chain with 19 stores. Besides presenting the company, it lets each store post its own job openings and delivers supplier messages straight to the right buyer.

story.problem: The chain needed a website that did real work, not just a brochure. Each store's HR staff had to post and manage their own job openings without touching another store's listings, and suppliers had no reliable way to reach the right person in purchasing.
story.solution: I built the site from scratch on WordPress, without page builders or form plugins. Each HR person logs in and sees only their store's openings. Candidates apply to a specific store and role, and the application goes to that store. Supplier messages are sorted by product category and delivered to the buyer responsible for it.
story.result: The site is live and in daily use: 22 HR staff manage openings for 19 stores and 2 distribution centers, and supplier messages land in the right inbox without anyone forwarding them.

bullets: A careers page where each store posts and manages its own job openings
Three access levels: store HR, HR managers who see every store, and site administrators
Applications go to the right store automatically, based on city and role
A supplier contact form that delivers each message to the buyer for that product category, with spam protection
Four custom admin screens, so the team can update stores and content without a developer
Each job posting gets its Google search description written automatically
A one-click maintenance mode that hides the site from visitors while changes are made
tech: Three-tier custom RBAC across 22 HR accounts — store-scoped "RH", store-agnostic "RH Admin", and extended Administrator caps, enforced via map_meta_cap, pre_get_posts query scoping, and admin-menu pruning
Category-based vendor routing: submissions matched against a configurable category→buyer→email map, guarded by reCAPTCHA v2, a honeypot, and a submission-timing check
Dynamic jobs board on a purpose-built custom post type, matching applications by city + role to the right store's contact email at submit time
Four custom wp-admin dashboards built without any admin-page framework, with AJAX store editing and IBGE municipality data synced via a build-time fetch script
Automated per-posting SEO metadata generation into Yoast fields, with a one-time backfill migration for existing content
Site-wide maintenance kill switch — assigning one template to the front page redirects all logged-out traffic, fully reversible, no plugin required

live.title: BPAgenda — Shared Expenses & Personal Organizer
live.description: An app for splitting expenses with friends and family that grew into a personal organizer: task boards, a focus timer, practice routines and a calendar. I use it every day with the people around me.

story.problem: I split bills with friends on Splitwise and outgrew its free plan. I also needed things it didn't do well: purchases paid in installments, bills that repeat every month, and a clear total for each month.
story.solution: So I built my own. You add an expense, choose how to split it, and the app keeps a running balance with each friend. From there I added the other tools I was juggling: shared task boards, a Pomodoro focus timer, timed practice routines and a calendar that links them all.
story.result: It's in daily use, works in English and Portuguese, and installs on a phone like a regular app.

bullets: Split any expense equally, fully on one person, or in custom amounts
Installment purchases and monthly bills are added automatically
A live balance with each friend that stays correct even after you edit or delete an expense
Shared task boards where you decide who can view and who can edit
A focus timer with ready-made or custom work-and-break cycles
Practice routines split into timed blocks, like an hour of guitar divided into scales, harmony and improvisation
Learns your categories: correct an expense once and it remembers next time
tech: Automated balance engine nets four aggregated sums (bidirectional debts + settlements) into a live per-friend balance on every read — nothing cached or denormalized, so totals stay correct after edits or deletions

Three-mode splitting (equal / full / custom) with multi-month installments and recurring monthly expenses generated inside atomic DB transactions, plus a validator that cross-checks friendship, payer/participant conflicts, and split-sum overflow before persisting
Hand-rolled 4-tier permission ladder (owner/full/read-write/read) gating every kanban mutation at the controller layer, on Laravel Sanctum SPA token auth
Collaborative lists with an append-only activity log that reconstructs every add/remove/check by diffing item arrays on each save
Self-hosted CI/CD — GitHub Actions deploys to a Docker/Nginx/MySQL VPS on every push to main; the frontend ships as an installable PWA with a Workbox service worker for offline-aware API caching
Self-learning categorization: a 21-category keyword-matching engine backed by a per-user "learned icon" table that remembers corrections and tracks usage

live.title: BHelper — Band Management App
live.description: An app for bands: setlists, the songs each member needs to practice, rehearsal plans and music tools, all in one place. Each band gets its own private space.

story.problem: I play in several bands, and our setlists, the songs we needed to work on and our rehearsal plans were scattered across chats, notes and spreadsheets. Nothing kept them together for the whole band.
story.solution: BHelper gives each band a private workspace with task boards, shared setlists and a song library. Add a song and it fills in the tempo, key and lyrics for you. It also has a tuner, a scale chart and a public page for each band.
story.result: It's live and used by my bands and by friends' bands, and new features come from their feedback.

bullets: A private workspace for each band; members only see the bands they belong to
Shared setlists and task boards for rehearsals
Add a song and its tempo, key and lyrics are filled in automatically
Turn a setlist into a streaming playlist, connecting your account by scanning a QR code with your phone
A precise instrument tuner that runs in the browser with your microphone
A fretboard chart for 30+ scales and a circle of fifths with chord suggestions
A public page for each band
tech: Header-verified multi-tenancy — every endpoint resolves the active band from a request header, checks it against verified membership server-side, and scopes every query; cross-band access returns 403 rather than trusting a client-supplied ID
OAuth (PKCE) with cross-device handoff — connect a streaming account from your phone via QR code while the desktop session polls for completion, then export a setlist directly into a new playlist
Automated metadata enrichment — new songs hydrated with BPM, key, and lyrics by orchestrating two external music APIs, with response caching to avoid redundant calls
Real-time in-browser tuner using Web Audio sampling, autocorrelation, and parabolic interpolation for sub-cent accuracy
CI/CD with deploy verification — GitHub Actions deploys on every push to main, verifying the deployed commit SHA and running a live HTTP health check before marking success
Unit-tested music-theory core — pitch detection and scale/transposition isolated into pure modules with ~390 lines of Vitest coverage, decoupled from the Web Audio/DOM layer

live.title: VPS Monitor — Server Health Dashboard
live.description: A private dashboard that watches every site and app I host, alerts my phone the moment something goes down, and shows how much room the server has left.

story.problem: I discovered that a site I host had been down for three weeks, and its database for two months, and nothing had warned me. The only checks I had ran when I published an update, and that project was never updated.
story.solution: VPS Monitor checks every service on the server once a minute, on its own schedule. It records every update I publish, shows how much processing power, memory and disk each app uses, and sends a notification to my phone when an update finishes or a service goes down.
story.result: 11 services are watched around the clock. An outage now reaches my phone within minutes, and decisions like whether the server can take another app are made from real numbers instead of guesses.

bullets: Checks 11 services every minute, however often they're updated
One alert when something goes down, then a daily reminder until it's fixed: no flood of messages
A 14-day uptime history for each service
A record of every update published to the server and whether it succeeded
Shows what each app costs in processing power, memory and disk
Simple OK / Watch / Act signals, such as how many more apps the memory can take
Built so it can never show "all good" by mistake: if its own checks stop running, it says so
tech: Health probes every minute on 11 services (container state plus a live HTTP check), whether or not a project has CI/CD, so a quiet service can no longer pass for a healthy one
Incident state machine: an outage opens only after consecutive failed checks, alerts once, and reminds daily while it stays open. A three-week outage is one alert and a daily nudge, not ~30,000 pings

Deploy tracking with no workflow changes: a GitHub App on all repositories sends signed webhooks (HMAC SHA-256); each run is classed as deployed, failed, tests failed or health check failed from the job that broke, and runs that never report back are closed as unknown

Least-privilege resource agent in plain Python, reading /proc and cgroups every 3s as nobody, on a read-only filesystem with no capabilities, reaching Docker only through a read-only socket proxy. Compose stacks, containers and systemd services are discovered, not configured

A disk breakdown that adds up: a sandboxed sizer (read-only root mount, no network, one capability) assigns every gigabyte to an app, Docker leftovers or the system, so the parts never add up to more than the disk

Capacity planning: OK / Watch / Act indicators for memory headroom, CPU p95, pressure-stall time, swap-in, CPU steal, reclaimable Docker disk, containers without memory limits and OOM kills, with 24h / 7d / 30d history
Its own deploy fails unless a probe ran in the last five minutes, and the status endpoint is never served from the PWA cache, because a stale board of green tiles would bring back the original bug

live.title: My Own Production Server — Hosting & Publishing
live.description: Instead of paying for separate hosting for every project, I run my apps and client sites, this portfolio included, on one server I set up and manage myself.

story.problem: Every project needs a home: a secure web address, email, a database and a safe way to publish updates. Paying for and managing separate hosting for each one wasn't worth it.
story.solution: I set up a single Linux server (2 processors, 4 GB of memory) as a production host. It serves 12 secure sites, sends email for the apps, keeps each app's data separate, and publishes updates automatically every time I send new code, checking that the site still works before calling it done.
story.result: 12 sites run on one small server, 8 projects update themselves automatically, and VPS Monitor tells me when something needs attention.

bullets: 12 sites on secure HTTPS, with certificates that renew themselves
Automatic publishing for 8 projects: send new code and the server updates, then confirms the site is working
Separate test and live versions for projects that need them
Its own email service, so apps can send messages that reach the inbox
A separate database for each app, so a problem in one never affects another
Automatic security updates, with capacity decisions made from real usage data
tech: nginx as the single TLS edge for 12 sites: Let's Encrypt certificates renewed by Certbot, HTTP to HTTPS redirects, one shared security-headers snippet, and year-long immutable caching for static assets

Mixed runtime on one box: 20 containers across Docker Compose stacks (Laravel, WordPress and other app stacks) beside native systemd services (PHP 8.4-FPM, MariaDB, a queue worker) and a Java game server

One deploy pattern across 8 repositories: GitHub Actions connects over SSH, resets the server to the exact pushed commit, stops if the SHA doesn't match, and only marks success after a live HTTPS health check. Separate staging and production where needed, and test-gated deploys for BHelper

Send-only mail server (Postfix + OpenDKIM in Docker): DKIM-signed mail relayed through Resend because the provider blocks outbound port 25. Each app gets its own SMTP login, can only send as its own address, and reaches the server on an internal Docker network
A database server per Docker stack (MySQL 8.0 / 8.4, MariaDB, PostgreSQL 16), so a bad migration or a crash in one app never touches another app's data
Swap sized for 4 GB of RAM, unattended security upgrades, log rotation, and memory limits, Docker disk cleanup and capacity decisions made from VPS Monitor's numbers

internal.title: Rede Zeferino — Store Operations System
internal.description: The internal system a supermarket chain's staff use every day to record deliveries, print labels, monitor store equipment and pull reports, connected to the company's main business software.

story.problem: Store operations depended on several separate systems: the inventory system (Oracle RMS), the business management system (Senior ERP) and local databases. Day-to-day tasks needed one place that could work with all of them.
story.solution: I designed and built one web system that brings these tasks together, alone and from scratch, including the framework it runs on. It reads and writes directly to the company's main systems, so what staff record shows up wherever it's needed. Each person sees only the screens their role allows.
story.result: In daily use across 8+ stores, handling more than 100 delivery check-ins a day, with updates published automatically and no downtime.

bullets: Records the weight of incoming goods in real time and prints the delivery report
Generates product labels and production reports
Shows whether each store's scales are online, with green, yellow and red status
Moves data between the company's systems
Each user sees only the screens their role allows, adjustable person by person
Light and dark modes
tech: Multi-database abstraction layer: one app talking to local MySQL, centralized Arius MySQL, Oracle RMS (read/write), and Oracle Senior ERP
Data-driven RBAC: permission classes with per-user overrides, a centralized access gate in the routing layer, and a dynamic sidebar rendered from a functionality catalog
Weight management workflow (Balança CP): real-time weight recording with immediate Oracle MERGE persistence, sequential numbering, verification, and romaneio report generation
Store monitoring: network status of scales across 8+ stores via SSH
CI/CD: GitHub Actions with a self-hosted Windows runner and PowerShell-automated zero-downtime deployments
Docker dev environment with Oracle Instant Client, MariaDB, Apache, and one-command startup
Dark/light theme system (CSS custom properties + Bootstrap 5.3 data-bs-theme, localStorage persistence, OS preference detection)

Dockerized environment with automatic port detection
